commenti.body:
Some insight from [Martin Scorsese](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/review-martin-scorsese-searchers-426059/):

>Ethan Edwards as brought to life by Wayne and Ford is a cousin to Melville’s Ahab on one hand and his Bartleby on the other — driven to the point of madness and absolutely alone.

>...

>For some, the frontier-comedy scenes with Ken Curtis are tough to take, but again, I don’t think they mar the film; these interludes are as much a part of the director’s universe as Shakespeare’s clowns are a part of his. For me, the problem was with the scenes involving a plump Comanche woman (Beulah Archuletta) that the Hunter character inadvertently takes as a wife. There is some low comedy in these scenes: Hunter kicks her down a hill, and Max Steiner’s score amplifies the moment with a comic flourish. Then the tone shifts dramatically, and Wayne and Hunter both become ruthless and bullying, scaring her away. Later, they find her body in a Comanche camp that has been wiped out by American soldiers, and you can feel their sense of loss. All the same, this passage seemed unnecessarily cruel to me. But the last time I saw The Searchers, the picture seemed even greater than ever, and it’s not that the scene had stopped troubling me; in fact, it troubled me on an even deeper level. In truly great films — the ones that people need to make, the ones that start speaking through them, the ones that keep moving into territory that is more and more unfathomable and uncomfortable — nothing’s ever simple or neatly resolved. You’re left with a mystery. In this case, the mystery of a man who spends 10 years of his life searching for someone, realizes his goal, brings her back and then walks away. Only an artist as great as John Ford would dare to end a film on such a note.

I think a lot of the plot is deliberately ambiguous so that the various interactions with Ethan and various members of society stand out.

I think a post JAWS summer blockbuster era, but not only are plots spelled out, but character arcs are attached to those plots.

I'll take something that's relatively contemporary like The Avengers..(2012)

While mostly an ensemble peace, and I think one can quickly discern Bruce Banner / the Hulk as being a bit of the main character.. he gets recruited early, and has the emotional journey go from destruction to acceptance.

It actually isn't a bad arc, but  I bring it up as a quick example of how commercial filmmaking generally is designed to push character stories in between action beats.

I mean this was true of swashbucklers, comedies, and Westerns back in the day- the awkward Clark Kent duality in Tyrone Power's Mark of Zorro, or the rapid fire dialog in His Girl Friday, or the real-time suspense in High Noon.

But I think in a lot of older movies, the character beats aren't attached to the plot-per say, but other character interactions. 

Ethan drawing up a will to Martin as someone who doesn't seem to show much external respect is probably less an act of genuine kindness, and more of a way of cutting his niece out of his life. 

And I think the trouble is when watching films that go from A to B, I think it becomes a barely subconscious thing of thinking of it as the only way to tell a story and not a way to avoid plodding around ( which occasionally can also lead to good storytelling) 

So I think when films do stylistically divergent things like have the Xanadu newsreel to fast forward through Charles Foster Kane's whole life, or have Vertigo have a lot of the story involving tracking a character and connecting bits and pieces of the plot, or have a dead body narrate the story ( Sunset Boulevard)  a lot of the criticisms that stated by modern audiences, and you could actually see in print critics back in the day.. 

I think Variety is a long enough running magazine to have old archived reviews. 

And so I think the knee jerk response of " this isn't logical" or "this isn't fun" it's something that treats the cinema art as a bit more pulp novelistic and not more lyrical like a music composition ( I think Kubrick made this analogy of music versus fiction) 

So I think with The Searchers ( referred to being an influence of the amazing Lawrence of Arabia)  it's as much of a celebration of the capabilities of the movie technology ( in towering Vista Vision)  as it is the character study of John Wayne's portrayal. 

I think humans as modern viewers tend to dislike unexpected elements of ambiguity. 

A quick example would be the fort and the victims of indigenous kidnapping. The insanity from the emotional trauma is perceived as a loss of the White identity by the men in the scene. 

I think this is an ambiguous scene, because I don't think one is a personal viewer should decipher this as being anything less than a psychotic break from the characters. 

Also a thing to note is the articulation and loyalty that Debbie has to the Comanche - - she's not a blank slate like the girls in the fort, but  rather a self-determined character. 

And so I think it's a film that is rough in places, because in some ways it allows John Wayne to invade a village with indigenous civilians with the consequence being his own moral limits, one he's willing to cross multiple times in the movie. 

I think that's why it's so challenging, it's not really an open and shut type plot- perhaps it's just a fever dream of grandeur.

I think he misses the point of the Look scenes. She's made fun of, she's kicked down the hill and we're supposed to laugh at her expense, but then she's found dead killed by the calvary. Marty even asks why they killed her, she didn't do anything. So, as viewers, don't we feel bad and ashamed now?

Scorsese’s Melville analogy is apt here. Part of the “point” is precisely that we’re following characters on a journey away from society, human connection and their accompanying ethical rules and boundaries. Ethan Allen, like Bartleby, would “prefer not to” live by those rules.
Please read my post carefully. I was only referring to the Look scenes.

I love Classic movies, especially Westerns, but The Searchers is not a good film. I completely understand why directors like Scorsese love it, but man what a mess. The film goes from ultra-serious to slapstick quicker than Wayne is with his iron. That neither is handled particularly well makes matters worse. Just look at Wayne's turn from a racist to a racist with a heart of gold. It comes out of nowhere and neither Wayne nor Ford seem interested in the moment. Then there is the comedy which was even old fashioned in 1956.
